meta.description: Wilde never sent it. The one-character exchange is an anonymous 1850 newspaper joke; Victor Hugo's name was attached in 1892, Wilde's not until 2013.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Briefest Correspondence: Question Mark? Exclamation Mark!'?
meta.ogDescription: An anonymous 1850 newspaper filler, not Oscar Wilde. The original reply was a cipher '0' meaning 'None' — the exclamation mark arrived with Victor Hugo in 1892.

answer.label: Not Oscar Wilde — an anonymous Victorian newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: Unsigned newspaper filler · earliest known printing 25 April 1850
answer.sourceLine: No letter, cable or telegram from Oscar Wilde containing a single question mark has ever been produced. The one-character exchange is a nameless comic filler that ran in British papers from April 1850; Victor Hugo’s name was attached to it in 1892, and Wilde’s name does not appear on it in any source earlier than 2013.

source.excerpt:
But the shortest correspondence ever known took place between Victor Hugo and his publisher, just after the publication of “Les Misérables.” The poet, impatient to learn of the success of the book, sent off a letter which contained only the following:

?

and he received the following entirely satisfactory answer:

!
trail: Quote Investigator traces the joke to an unsigned “Varieties” filler in The Nottinghamshire Guardian of 25 April 1850, in which no one is named and the reply is a cipher, and follows it through English and American papers into the 1850s. Quote Investigator ↗

Frederick Saunders’ Pastime Papers was still telling it with no names in 1885: on page 37, in the chapter “Letters and Letter-Writing,” the query “?” means “Is there any news?” and the answer is “a cipher (o) — None.” Pastime Papers, R. Bentley & Son, 1885 ↗

Victor Hugo enters in Walsh’s Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities. The passage is readable in full in the Internet Archive’s scan, a J. B. Lippincott printing dated 1893; Quote Investigator cites the 1892 edition, page 600. Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities ↗
Wikipedia files the whole story under apocrypha, noting the sender is “variously identified as Victor Hugo or Oscar Wilde,” and cites Quote Investigator as its only source. Telegram style ↗
source.excerptNote: Walsh’s is the earliest known printing to attach a real writer’s name to the joke, and the earliest to give the reply as an exclamation mark. Quote Investigator notes the thirty-year delay after Les Misérables and treats the Hugo version as doubtful. In the 1850 newspaper item and in Saunders’ Pastime Papers of 1885 the correspondents are anonymous and the answer is a cipher, “0,” meaning “None.”

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted for this line, because there is no work to attach one to. The Victorian texts the anecdote descends from are all long out of copyright — the 1850 newspaper filler, Saunders’ Pastime Papers (1885) and Walsh’s Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities (1892), which the Internet Archive marks as not in copyright. But the sentence as it circulates, “Briefest Correspondence: Question Mark? Exclamation Mark!”, is not a period wording at all: it is the headline Quote Investigator gave its own 2014 article about the story, so no pre-1931 work contains it.

author.name: William S. Walsh
author.heading: The man who handed the story to Victor Hugo
author.metaLine: 1854–1919 · American editor and compiler of literary curiosities
author.bio: William Shepard Walsh was an American editor and anthologist whose Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities (J. B. Lippincott, 1892) gathered hundreds of literary oddities, hoaxes and coincidences into a single alphabetical compendium. He did not invent the “?”/“!” joke — it was already in print four years before he was born — but his book is the earliest known printing that pins it on a real writer, and every later telling descends from that page, including the Guinness Book’s and, eventually, Oscar Wilde’s.

cite.sourceCitation: William S. Walsh, Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities (Philadelphia: J. B. Lippincott, 1892), 600 — the earliest known printing to name Victor Hugo. The joke itself is older and anonymous: the earliest printing known to Quote Investigator is “Varieties,” The Nottinghamshire Guardian (Nottinghamshire, England), 25 April 1850, p. 4, where nobody is named and the reply is a cipher, “0.” No source connects the exchange to Oscar Wilde before 2013.

copyAttribution: Not Oscar Wilde. The one-character "?"/"!" exchange is an anonymous newspaper joke, first printed in The Nottinghamshire Guardian on 25 April 1850 — with a cipher "0" as the reply, not an exclamation mark. Victor Hugo's name was attached to it in 1892, in William S. Walsh's Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities; Oscar Wilde's name does not appear on it before 2013. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: The exchange has been in print for well over a century and a half, and it has picked up a different celebrity at almost every stop. Each new name arrives later than the last, and none arrives with a document.

items.why: The earliest Wilde telling Quote Investigator could find is dated 2013 — a business-communication handbook, more than a century after the story was already in print under other names, and with no letter, cable or publisher named. QI’s verdict on it is blunt: it “has no substantive support.” Quote Investigator ↗

items.scope: The classic telling, and the Guinness Book version
items.why: Hugo’s name first appears in Walsh’s 1892 Handy-Book, thirty years after Les Misérables, and the 1981 Guinness Book of World Records repeated it as a record, naming the publisher as Hurst and Blackett. That was the London house that issued the first British translation in October 1862 — not A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven & Cie of Brussels, who actually published the novel on 31 March 1862. Les Misérables ↗

items.who: An unnamed correspondent, then an American merchant
items.why: In the earliest versions nobody famous is involved at all: an anonymous pair in 1850, and by September 1854 “an American merchant in want of news and his London agent” — and the reply is a cipher, not an exclamation mark. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody sent it. Quote Investigator concludes that all of these tales of brief correspondence were fictional, published simply to amuse readers — and every famous name on the story arrived decades after the joke was already in circulation. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: A joke that keeps recasting itself
lead: The appeal is structural. Two marks of punctuation carry a whole conversation — anxiety and triumph, author and publisher — and the reader supplies everything in between. That is why the story survives: it is not really an anecdote about anyone, it is a party trick about how little language you need, and it works exactly as well with any famous name dropped into it.

Which is also why it keeps drifting. In 1850 the correspondents are nobody. By 1854 they are an American merchant and his London agent. By 1892 the sender is Victor Hugo. By 1981 the Guinness Book of World Records is printing it as a record, with a date and a publisher attached. By 2013 the sender is Oscar Wilde. Nothing about the exchange changed; only the celebrity did.
context.detailsSummary: How the punchline flipped from “0” to “!”
detailsBody: The original gag is bleaker and funnier than the version people repeat. In the 1850 newspaper item, and still in Frederick Saunders’ Pastime Papers in 1885, the query “?” means “Is there any news?” and the answer is a cipher — a zero — meaning “None.” It is a joke about silence.

The exclamation mark arrives with the Victor Hugo telling in 1892, and it changes the whole point: the reply is now enthusiasm rather than emptiness, which is what makes it usable as a flattering story about a bestseller. A September 1854 American printing had already swapped the marks the other way round, opening with “!” and answering “0.” The characters were never fixed, which is a fair sign nobody was transcribing a real document.
context.pull: Nobody sent it. The joke arrived first and collected its famous names afterwards.

sourcesVerified.claim: Earliest known printing is an unsigned item in The Nottinghamshire Guardian, 25 April 1850, with '?' meaning 'Is there any news?' answered by a cipher '0' meaning 'None'; the Victor Hugo version first appears in Walsh's 1892 Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities, p. 600, thirty years after Les Misérables; the 1981 Guinness Book of World Records retold it naming Hurst and Blackett and 1862; the earliest Oscar Wilde version is dated 2013 (Theo Theobald, On Message, p. 27); QI concludes all such tales were fictional and that the Wilde variant 'has no substantive support'; a September 1854 Portland Weekly Advertiser version used '!' answered by '0' and named an American merchant and his London agent.

The Internet Archive scan of William S. Walsh's Handy-Book of Literary Curiosities (J. B. Lippincott, Philadelphia; item dated 1893, author Walsh, William Shepard, 1854-1919, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT and freely readable) contains the passage: 'But the shortest correspondence ever known took place between Victor Hugo and his publisher, just after the publication of "Les Miserables." The poet, impatient to learn of the success of the book, sent off a letter which contained only the following: ?'

Frederick Saunders (1807-1902), Pastime Papers (London: R. Bentley & Son, 1885), freely readable and marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, contains on page 37 in the chapter 'Letters and Letter-Writing': 'In the briefest correspondence known, only two figures were used: the first contained a note of interrogation (?) — implying, Is there any news? The answer was a cipher (o) — None.' — no names, and no exclamation mark.

Wikipedia describes the story as apocryphal: 'An apocryphal story about the briefest correspondence in history has a writer (variously identified as Victor Hugo or Oscar Wilde) inquiring about the sales of his new book by sending the message "?" to his publisher, and receiving "!" in reply,' citing Quote Investigator's 2014 article as its source.

Les Misérables was published on 31 March 1862 in Belgium by A. Lacroix, Verboeckhoven & Cie; the first British translation was published by Hurst and Blackett in October 1862, translated by Lascelles Wraxall.

Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde page contains no reference anywhere — including its Disputed and Misattributed sections — to Wilde sending a telegram or letter containing only a question mark to his publisher and receiving an exclamation mark in reply.
